claim: Planar cell polarity (PCP) and neural tube defects (NTDs) are linked, with a subset of NTD patients found to harbor mutations in PCP genes.
source: Planar cell polarity (PCP) and neural tube defects (NTDs) are linked, with a subset of NTD patients found to harbor mutations in PCP genes, but there is limited data on whether these mutations disrupt PCP signaling in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to existing literature establishing the link between PCP mutations and NTDs in patient populations.

claim: There is limited data on whether NTD-associated mutations in PCP genes disrupt PCP signaling in vivo.
source: Planar cell polarity (PCP) and neural tube defects (NTDs) are linked, with a subset of NTD patients found to harbor mutations in PCP genes, but there is limited data on whether these mutations disrupt PCP signaling in vivo.
evidence: The authors state this as a gap in current knowledge that motivates their study.

claim: Van Gogh (Vang), Vangl1/2 in mammals, is the most specific core PCP gene for PCP.
source: The core PCP gene Van Gogh (Vang), Vangl1/2 in mammals, is the most specific for PCP.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the specificity of Vang/Vangl genes for PCP signaling.

claim: Introducing mammalian Vangl1/2 mutations into Drosophila Vang revealed defective phenotypic and functional behaviors.
source: Introducing the respective mammalian mutations into Drosophila Vang revealed defective phenotypic and functional behaviors, with changes to Vang localization, post-translational modification, and mechanistic function, such as its ability to interact with PCP effectors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mammalian Vangl1/2 mutations introduced into Drosophila Vang caused changes to Vang localization.
source: Introducing the respective mammalian mutations into Drosophila Vang revealed defective phenotypic and functional behaviors, with changes to Vang localization, post-translational modification, and mechanistic function, such as its ability to interact with PCP effectors.
evidence: This finding is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Mammalian Vangl1/2 mutations introduced into Drosophila Vang caused changes to post-translational modification of Vang.
source: Introducing the respective mammalian mutations into Drosophila Vang revealed defective phenotypic and functional behaviors, with changes to Vang localization, post-translational modification, and mechanistic function, such as its ability to interact with PCP effectors.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing altered protein mobility and phosphorylation status in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mammalian Vangl1/2 mutations introduced into Drosophila Vang affected the ability of Vang to interact with PCP effectors.
source: Introducing the respective mammalian mutations into Drosophila Vang revealed defective phenotypic and functional behaviors, with changes to Vang localization, post-translational modification, and mechanistic function, such as its ability to interact with PCP effectors.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Each human mutation analyzed is a causative factor for the associated NTD.
source: Importantly, analyses of the human mutations revealed that each is a causative factor for the associated NTD.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the functional analyses showing that all human mutations tested cause PCP defects in Drosophila.

claim: Neural tube closure defects (NTDs) affect approximately 1 in 1000 births in humans.
source: Neural tube closure defects (NTDs) are common congenital malformations in humans, affecting approximately 1 in 1000 births.
evidence: This is a cited epidemiological fact about NTD prevalence.

claim: During embryogenesis, the neural plate undergoes shaping, before neural folds develop and elevate, contact, and then fuse at the midline to create the closed tube structure that will form the spinal cord and brain.
source: During embryogenesis, the neural plate undergoes shaping, before neural folds develop and elevate, contact, and then fuse at the midline to create the closed tube structure that will form the spinal cord and brain (Copp et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the normal developmental process of neural tube closure, supported by citation.

claim: Studies in Xenopus, zebrafish, and subsequently mouse revealed a role for planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling in neural tube closure.
source: Studies in Xenopus, zebrafish, and subsequently mouse, revealed a role for planar cell polarity (PCP) signaling in this process.
evidence: This is supported by references to previous studies in model organisms.

claim: Looptail (Lp) mice with mutations in the mVangl2 locus fail to establish a neural plate width that will allow for bending and closure.
source: Further, it was demonstrated that Looptail (Lp) mice, with mutations in the mVangl2 locus (see below), fail to establish a neural plate width that will allow for bending and closure (Etheridge et al., 2008; Wallingford and Harland, 2002; Wang et al., 2006a; Ybot-Gonzalez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies of the Looptail mouse model.

claim: Vangl2 is expressed broadly in the neural plate prior to, during, and after closure.
source: Consistent with a role in neurulation, Vangl2 (an orthologue of the Drosophila PCP core gene Van Gogh/Vang) is expressed broadly in the neural plate prior to, during, and after closure (Kibar et al., 2001).
evidence: This expression pattern is supported by citation to Kibar et al., 2001.

claim: Vangl1 is expressed in the neural plate tissue with a more restricted pattern showing a complementary pattern with Vangl2.
source: Interestingly, the second orthologous mouse gene, Vangl1, is also expressed in this tissue; however, its expression is more restricted, showing a complementary pattern with Vangl2 (Doudney et al., 2005; Torban et al., 2008; Torban et al., 2007).
evidence: This expression pattern is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Looptail was originally defined by two independent mutations (D255E and S464N) in mVangl2 that map to the C-terminal tail.
source: Lp was originally defined by two independent mutations (D255E and S464N) in mVangl2 that map to the C-terminal tail.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the genetic basis of the Looptail phenotype.

claim: Both Looptail mutations (D255E and S464N) display an identical phenotype, with homozygous mice developing craniorachischisis, a completely open neural tube.
source: Both display an identical phenotype, with homozygous mice developing craniorachischisis, a completely open neural tube (Kibar et al., 2001; Murdoch et al., 2001).
evidence: This phenotypic description is supported by citations to the original studies.

claim: The Looptail mutations were found to disrupt binding between Vangl2 and effectors.
source: At the molecular level, the mutations were found to disrupt binding between Vangl2 and effectors and also showed reduced membrane localization, decreased protein levels, and defective phosphorylation of Vangl2 (Devenport and Fuchs, 2008; Gao et al., 2011; Guyot et al., 2011; Murdoch et al., 2014; Song et al., 2010; Torban et al., 2004; Torban et al., 2007).
evidence: This molecular characterization is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Looptail mutations showed reduced membrane localization of Vangl2.
source: At the molecular level, the mutations were found to disrupt binding between Vangl2 and effectors and also showed reduced membrane localization, decreased protein levels, and defective phosphorylation of Vangl2 (Devenport and Fuchs, 2008; Gao et al., 2011; Guyot et al., 2011; Murdoch et al., 2014; Song et al., 2010; Torban et al., 2004; Torban et al., 2007).
evidence: This molecular characterization is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Looptail mutations showed decreased protein levels of Vangl2.
source: At the molecular level, the mutations were found to disrupt binding between Vangl2 and effectors and also showed reduced membrane localization, decreased protein levels, and defective phosphorylation of Vangl2 (Devenport and Fuchs, 2008; Gao et al., 2011; Guyot et al., 2011; Murdoch et al., 2014; Song et al., 2010; Torban et al., 2004; Torban et al., 2007).
evidence: This molecular characterization is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Looptail mutations showed defective phosphorylation of Vangl2.
source: At the molecular level, the mutations were found to disrupt binding between Vangl2 and effectors and also showed reduced membrane localization, decreased protein levels, and defective phosphorylation of Vangl2 (Devenport and Fuchs, 2008; Gao et al., 2011; Guyot et al., 2011; Murdoch et al., 2014; Song et al., 2010; Torban et al., 2004; Torban et al., 2007).
evidence: This molecular characterization is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The molecular characterization of Looptail mutations led to suggestions that the mutants are loss-of-function (LOF).
source: Overall, this led to suggestions that the mutants are loss-of-function (LOF), and that Vangl2 is a rate-limiting component in a dosage-sensitive pathway.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the molecular data from previous studies.

claim: Vangl2 is a rate-limiting component in a dosage-sensitive pathway.
source: Overall, this led to suggestions that the mutants are loss-of-function (LOF), and that Vangl2 is a rate-limiting component in a dosage-sensitive pathway.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the genetic and molecular data from Looptail studies.

claim: The earliest genetic studies of Looptail suggested a semi-dominant mutation with incomplete penetrance.
source: However, this is in contrast to the earliest genetic studies, which suggested a semi-dominant mutation with incomplete penetrance.
evidence: This refers to the original genetic characterization of the Looptail allele.

claim: The majority of, but not all, Looptail heterozygotes show a looped tail phenotype caused by delay of posterior neuropore closure.
source: This was due to the presence of a looped tail phenotype in the majority of, but not all heterozygotes, caused by delay of posterior neuropore closure (Copp et al., 1994; Strong and Hollander, 1949).
evidence: This phenotypic observation is supported by citations to early genetic studies.

claim: Other PCP mutant mice were found to develop NTDs, implicating pathway defects as a disease risk factor.
source: Since the original identification of the Vangl2Lp alleles, other PCP mutant mice were found to develop NTDs, implicating the pathway defects as a disease risk factor (Andre et al., 2012; Curtin et al., 2003; Etheridge et al., 2008; Hamblet et al., 2002; Merte et al., 2010; Murdoch et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2006a; Wang et al., 2006b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies of PCP mutant mice.

claim: A number of mutations were identified in patient populations in VANGL1 and VANGL2, as well as additional core PCP and associated proteins.
source: A number of mutations were identified in patient populations in VANGL1 and VANGL2, as well as additional core PCP and associated proteins (reviewed in Juriloff and Harris, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a review citation summarizing patient mutation studies.

claim: In each case of patient mutations, the mutation was heterozygous.
source: In each case, the mutation was heterozygous and, interestingly, familial mutations could be found to result in different disease severity among family members.
evidence: This is a factual observation about the genetic nature of patient mutations.

claim: Familial mutations in PCP genes could be found to result in different disease severity among family members.
source: In each case, the mutation was heterozygous and, interestingly, familial mutations could be found to result in different disease severity among family members.
evidence: This observation supports the complex etiology of NTDs.

claim: NTDs are thought to result from a mixture of genetic and environmental factors.
source: However, this is perhaps not surprising given the complex etiology of NTDs, which are thought to result from a mixture of genetic and environmental factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the multifactorial nature of NTDs.

claim: Digenic mutations were discovered among PCP genes in NTD patients.
source: Furthermore, digenic mutations were also discovered among PCP genes, consistent with a multifactorial hypothesis, whereby additional factors would be required to achieve a threshold for disease progression (Allache et al., 2012; Beaumont et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2018b; De Marco et al., 2012; Merello et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies identifying digenic mutations.

claim: Digenic mutations among PCP genes are consistent with a multifactorial hypothesis for NTD development.
source: Furthermore, digenic mutations were also discovered among PCP genes, consistent with a multifactorial hypothesis, whereby additional factors would be required to achieve a threshold for disease progression (Allache et al., 2012; Beaumont et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2018b; De Marco et al., 2012; Merello et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the digenic mutation data.

claim: Chimeric mouse studies using the Looptail allele showed an all-or-nothing effect in developing craniorachischisis.
source: This is additionally supported by chimeric mouse studies using the Lp allele that showed an all-or-nothing effect in developing craniorachischisis (Musci and Mullen, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a chimeric mouse study.

claim: Only a few studies have addressed whether PCP mutations identified in patients are pathological.
source: Despite the progress in identifying mutations within PCP components, data is lacking as to whether these mutations are in fact pathological, with only a few studies addressing this question to date (Iliescu et al., 2014; Kibar et al., 2007; Lei et al., 2010; Reynolds et al., 2010).
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Evidence has emerged that the mVangl2Lp allele may be a dominant negative mutation.
source: Furthermore, evidence has emerged that the mVangl2Lp allele may in fact be a dominant negative mutation (Song et al., 2010; Yin et al., 2012), indicating there is more to investigate surrounding its molecular behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies suggesting dominant negative behavior.

claim: A recessive mVangl2Lp mutation (R259L) gave an apparently normal phenotype in heterozygotes.
source: In addition, a recessive mVangl2Lp mutation was discovered (with substitution R259L) that gave an apparently normal phenotype in heterozygotes.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the R259L mutation phenotype.

claim: Only 47% of homozygote R259L animals displayed a looped tail and 12% developed spina bifida.
source: In this case, only 47% of homozygote animals displayed a looped tail and 12% developed spina bifida, a milder NTD as compared to craniorachischisis, leading to the suggestion that this Lp mutation is a hypomorphic Vangl2 LOF allele (Guyot et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2006b; Yin et al., 2012).
evidence: This phenotypic data is supported by citations.

claim: The R259L Looptail mutation is suggested to be a hypomorphic Vangl2 LOF allele.
source: In this case, only 47% of homozygote animals displayed a looped tail and 12% developed spina bifida, a milder NTD as compared to craniorachischisis, leading to the suggestion that this Lp mutation is a hypomorphic Vangl2 LOF allele (Guyot et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2006b; Yin et al., 2012).
evidence: This interpretation is based on the milder phenotype compared to other Looptail alleles.

claim: Polarization of epithelial cells is critical for the morphogenesis and function of mature tissues.
source: Polarization of epithelial cells, and cells in general, is critical for the morphogenesis and function of mature tissues, with perturbation of cellular polarity and tissue organization implicated in numerous diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the importance of cell polarity.

claim: Perturbation of cellular polarity and tissue organization is implicated in numerous diseases.
source: Polarization of epithelial cells, and cells in general, is critical for the morphogenesis and function of mature tissues, with perturbation of cellular polarity and tissue organization implicated in numerous diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of polarity defects in disease.

claim: Epithelial cell polarity can be derived in two axes: apical-basal and orthogonal to the plane of the epithelium (planar cell polarity).
source: Epithelial cell polarity can be derived in two axes, apical-basal and orthogonal to the plane of the epithelium, which is referred to as planar cell polarity (PCP).
evidence: This is a definition of the two types of epithelial polarity.

claim: PCP establishment is governed by members of the conserved non-canonical Wnt/Frizzled-PCP pathway.
source: PCP establishment is governed by members of the conserved non-canonical Wnt/Frizzled-PCP pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular basis of PCP.

claim: Vang was originally discovered in Drosophila, like all other core PCP factors.
source: Besides the four-pass trans-membrane protein Vang (Vangl1 and Vangl2 in mammals, see above), which was - like all other core PCP factors - originally discovered in Drosophila (Taylor et al., 1998), a.k.a. strabismus/stbm (Wolff and Rubin, 1998), they include the atypical cadherin Flamingo (Fmi; Celsr in mammals), the seven-pass transmembrane protein Frizzled (Fz; Fzd in vertebrates with several family members), and the cytoplasmic proteins Dishevelled (Dsh; Dvl in mammals), Diego (Dgo; Inversin/Diversin in vertebrates), and Prickle (Pk).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original Drosophila studies.

claim: Core PCP factors include Flamingo (Fmi; Celsr in mammals), Frizzled (Fz; Fzd in vertebrates), Dishevelled (Dsh; Dvl in mammals), Diego (Dgo; Inversin/Diversin in vertebrates), and Prickle (Pk).
source: Besides the four-pass trans-membrane protein Vang (Vangl1 and Vangl2 in mammals, see above), which was - like all other core PCP factors - originally discovered in Drosophila (Taylor et al., 1998), a.k.a. strabismus/stbm (Wolff and Rubin, 1998), they include the atypical cadherin Flamingo (Fmi; Celsr in mammals), the seven-pass transmembrane protein Frizzled (Fz; Fzd in vertebrates with several family members), and the cytoplasmic proteins Dishevelled (Dsh; Dvl in mammals), Diego (Dgo; Inversin/Diversin in vertebrates), and Prickle (Pk).
evidence: This lists the core components of the PCP pathway.

claim: The PCP pathway is synonymous with the asymmetric localization of core members, which form into two sub-complexes on opposite sides of a given cell.
source: The pathway is synonymous with the asymmetric localization of these core members, which form into two sub-complexes on opposite sides of a given cell, creating an intracellular bridge to convey polarity across the tissue.
evidence: This describes the fundamental mechanism of PCP signaling.

claim: PCP complexes direct spatially restricted downstream signaling through tissue-specific effectors, leading to cytoskeletal rearrangement in the majority of cases.
source: The complexes also direct spatially restricted downstream signaling through tissue-specific effectors, leading to cytoskeletal rearrangement in the majority of cases (Adler, 2012; Goodrich and Strutt, 2011; Humphries and Mlodzik, 2018; Singh and Mlodzik, 2012; Vladar et al., 2009; Yang and Mlodzik, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple review citations.

claim: Asymmetric localization of PCP complexes is directly observable in cells of the Drosophila wing where they align to the proximal-distal axis.
source: Asymmetric localization of PCP complexes is directly observable in cells of the Drosophila wing where they align to the proximal-distal axis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCP in the Drosophila wing.

claim: Molecular interactions promote the formation of stable complexes at proximal (Fmi-Vang-Pk) and distal (Fmi-Fz-Dsh-Dgo) cell membranes in the Drosophila wing.
source: Molecular interactions promote the formation of stable complexes at proximal (Fmi-Vang-Pk) and distal (Fmi-Fz-Dsh-Dgo) cell membranes, with Fmi forming a homotypic interaction across cells.
evidence: This describes the molecular organization of PCP complexes.

claim: Fmi forms a homotypic interaction across cells in PCP complexes.
source: Molecular interactions promote the formation of stable complexes at proximal (Fmi-Vang-Pk) and distal (Fmi-Fz-Dsh-Dgo) cell membranes, with Fmi forming a homotypic interaction across cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Flamingo/Celsr function in PCP.

claim: In the Drosophila wing, PCP signaling leads to the formation of a single-actin rich hair at the distal vertex of each cell.
source: In the wing, signaling leads to the formation of a single-actin rich hair at the distal vertex of each cell.
evidence: This is the visible readout of PCP in the wing.

claim: In the Drosophila eye, PCP signaling is responsible for determining the differential fate specification of photoreceptors R3 and R4.
source: For example, in the Drosophila eye, PCP signaling is responsible for determining the differential fate specification of photoreceptors R3 and R4, which also directs rotation and subsequent orientation of the photoreceptor clusters, referred to as ommatidia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCP function in the Drosophila eye.

claim: PCP signaling directs rotation and subsequent orientation of ommatidia in the Drosophila eye.
source: For example, in the Drosophila eye, PCP signaling is responsible for determining the differential fate specification of photoreceptors R3 and R4, which also directs rotation and subsequent orientation of the photoreceptor clusters, referred to as ommatidia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCP function in the Drosophila eye.

claim: PCP signaling leads to a mirror-image arrangement of ommatidia across the dorso-ventral midline (equator) in the Drosophila eye.
source: These signaling events in turn lead to a mirror-image arrangement of ommatidia across the dorso-ventral midline, or equator.
evidence: This is the visible readout of PCP in the eye.

claim: Disruption of PCP in the wing leads to misorientation of cellular hairs or multiple wing hairs.
source: Disruption of PCP in the wing leads to misorientation of cellular hairs or multiple wing hairs (Adler, 2012; Goodrich and Strutt, 2011; Humphries and Mlodzik, 2018; Singh and Mlodzik, 2012), while in the eye chirality or rotation defects of the ommatidia are observed (Mlodzik, 1999; Strutt and Strutt, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple review citations.

claim: Disruption of PCP in the eye leads to chirality or rotation defects of the ommatidia.
source: Disruption of PCP in the wing leads to misorientation of cellular hairs or multiple wing hairs (Adler, 2012; Goodrich and Strutt, 2011; Humphries and Mlodzik, 2018; Singh and Mlodzik, 2012), while in the eye chirality or rotation defects of the ommatidia are observed (Mlodzik, 1999; Strutt and Strutt, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of PCP in the eye.

claim: The PCP pathway is highly conserved in vertebrates.
source: The PCP pathway is highly conserved in vertebrates, with different tissues displaying PCP readouts or defects upon misregulation (Goodrich and Strutt, 2011; Wang and Nathans, 2007; Yang and Mlodzik, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by review citations.

claim: The study focused on six mutations located in the C-terminal tail of Vang.
source: Overall, we focused on six mutations located in the C-terminal tail of Vang, where all molecular interactions have been thus far mapped.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: All molecular interactions of Vang have been mapped to the C-terminal tail.
source: Overall, we focused on six mutations located in the C-terminal tail of Vang, where all molecular interactions have been thus far mapped.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Vang protein structure-function.

claim: All six mutations investigated resulted in aberrant PCP signaling and phenotypes.
source: We observed that all resulted in aberrant PCP signaling and phenotypes, however, to varying degrees.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figures 2-5.

claim: The six mutations investigated resulted in aberrant PCP signaling and phenotypes to varying degrees.
source: We observed that all resulted in aberrant PCP signaling and phenotypes, however, to varying degrees.
evidence: This is a primary finding showing differential effects of mutations.

claim: In the majority of cases, the mutations were dominant, either hypermorphic gain-of-function or dominant negative.
source: In the majority of cases, the mutation was dominant, either hypermorphic gain-of-function or dominant negative, leading to altered protein localization of both alleles in vivo.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figures 3-5.

claim: The dominant mutations led to altered protein localization of both alleles in vivo.
source: In the majority of cases, the mutation was dominant, either hypermorphic gain-of-function or dominant negative, leading to altered protein localization of both alleles in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3.

claim: One mutation (R321L) was shown to be hypomorphic in its behavior.
source: We were also able to show that one mutation was indeed hypomorphic in its behavior.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 2-5.

claim: The analyses demonstrate the causative association of the different VANGL1/2 alleles with the NTD phenotypes of human patient mutations.
source: Taken together, our analyses demonstrate in molecular detail the nature of the different VANGL1/2 alleles. These alleles display defective PCP signaling in vivo, indicating their causative association with the NTD phenotypes of the human patient mutations.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data.

claim: Mutations known to be causative for NTD in the mouse all map to the C-terminal tail of Vangl genes.
source: While mutations have been observed along the entire span of the VANGL1/2 genes in human NTD patients, mutations known to be causative for NTD in the mouse all map to the C-terminal tail (Chen et al., 2013; El-Hassan et al., 2018; Guyot et al., 2011; Kibar et al., 2001; Murdoch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to mouse studies.

claim: Vang interacts genetically with each PCP core gene.
source: Vang interacts genetically with each PCP core gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Vang function in PCP.

claim: Vang can physically interact with all other members of the PCP complex.
source: It has further been demonstrated that it also can physically interact with all other members of the PCP complex, and the interaction sites with the cytoplasmic PCP core factors have been mapped to its C-terminal domain (Bastock et al., 2003; Darken et al., 2002; Das et al., 2004; Humphries and Mlodzik, 2018; Jenny et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to biochemical studies.

claim: The interaction sites of Vang with cytoplasmic PCP core factors have been mapped to its C-terminal domain.
source: It has further been demonstrated that it also can physically interact with all other members of the PCP complex, and the interaction sites with the cytoplasmic PCP core factors have been mapped to its C-terminal domain (Bastock et al., 2003; Darken et al., 2002; Das et al., 2004; Humphries and Mlodzik, 2018; Jenny et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structure-function studies.

claim: The study selected two mutations from mouse (D255E and R259L) and four mutations from human patients (M328T, R517H, R270H, and R353C) for analysis.
source: For our study, we selected two mutations from the mouse and four mutations from human patients for further analysis, these include D255E and R259L identified in mouse Vangl2 (Guyot et al., 2011; Kibar et al., 2001), M328T and R517H found in human VANGL1 (Kibar et al., 2007; Merello et al., 2015), and R270H and R353C from human VANGL2 (Kibar et al., 2011; Lei et al., 2010; Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and mutation selection.

claim: The mouse D255E mutation is more conservative than R259L but displays a more severe phenotype in mouse models.
source: Firstly, we were interested to compare mouse D255E and R259L in a genetically uniform background, as the mutations are only a few residues apart, and strikingly the more conservative mutation (D255E) displays a more severe phenotype as compared to R259L in mouse models (Guyot et al., 2011; Kibar et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mouse studies.

claim: R270H was selected because the residue is absolutely conserved across all species.
source: Secondly, R270H was selected, as the residue is absolutely conserved across all species, and it covers two independent mutational events, as a mutation in VANGL1 was also observed at the equivalent residue (see Figure 1B) in a digenic combination along with a CELSR1 mutation (Chen et al., 2018a; Kibar et al., 2007).
evidence: This explains the rationale for selecting this mutation.

claim: A mutation at the residue equivalent to R270H was observed in VANGL1 in a digenic combination with a CELSR1 mutation.
source: Secondly, R270H was selected, as the residue is absolutely conserved across all species, and it covers two independent mutational events, as a mutation in VANGL1 was also observed at the equivalent residue (see Figure 1B) in a digenic combination along with a CELSR1 mutation (Chen et al., 2018a; Kibar et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to patient studies.

claim: Information to date suggests M328T may be a LOF allele.
source: Thirdly, M328T was chosen because information to date suggests this mutation may be a LOF allele (Reynolds et al., 2010), and R353C as it was suggested that effector binding may be reduced (Lei et al., 2010; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: It was suggested that R353C may have reduced effector binding.
source: Thirdly, M328T was chosen because information to date suggests this mutation may be a LOF allele (Reynolds et al., 2010), and R353C as it was suggested that effector binding may be reduced (Lei et al., 2010; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: R517H is a highly conserved residue with a conservative mutation where the bioinformatic prediction of its tolerance was unclear.
source: Finally, we selected R517H, a highly conserved residue with a conservative mutation where the bioinformatic prediction of its tolerance was unclear (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This explains the rationale for selecting this mutation.

claim: Driving expression of wild-type Vang with actin-Gal4 led to a moderate hair reorientation phenotype.
source: Driving expression of wild-type (wt-)Vang with actin-Gal4 (ac >WT) led to a moderate hair reorientation phenotype (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: D317E, R321L and K577H showed a distinct phenotype in region 1 as compared to wt-Vang overexpression.
source: In region 1, D317E, R321L and K577H showed a distinct phenotype as compared to wt-Vang (over)expression.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The hair pattern of D317E, R321L and K577H in region 1 was more similar to Vang-/- wings or a genetically wild-type wing (w1118).
source: In fact, their hair pattern was more similar to that of Vang-/- wings or a genetically wild-type wing (w1118), included as a reference control that has no phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2B.

claim: R332H, V391T and K418C showed hair reorientation patterns similar to the gain-of-function effect of wt-Vang overexpression in region 1.
source: In contrast, R332H, V391T and K418C all showed hair reorientation patterns similar to the gain-of-function (GOF) effect of wt-Vang overexpression (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In region 2, D317E and K577H mirrored the phenotype of Vang-/-.
source: In this case, D317E and K577H mirrored the phenotype of Vang-/-, while R321L showed similarity to the reference control (w1118).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In region 2, R321L showed similarity to the reference control (w1118).
source: In this case, D317E and K577H mirrored the phenotype of Vang-/-, while R321L showed similarity to the reference control (w1118).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In region 2, R332H, V391T and K418C showed similar patterns to the GOF overexpression of wt-Vang.
source: R332H, V391T and K418C again showed similar patterns to the GOF overexpression of wt-Vang (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
